passage:
Dear Karthik,

Remember the phone I said I "had to" upgrade? I did it: nothing down, twelve small EMIs, "only a few hundred a month". Then the headphones, then the jacket, each on its own tiny EMI. Last night I finally added them all in a note and the total surprised me. Small EMIs stack up quietly 😅

I asked myself the question you would ask: do I need it? Honestly, none of those was a need. They were a mood, and my friends' new things. So I've made a rule: any purchase waits a week. If I still want it after that, I look at the total cost, not the monthly figure. And no new EMI until two of these are cleared.

Thanks for not laughing when I told you.

Asif

qa.q: How many small EMIs did the phone purchase involve?
qa.a: The phone came with twelve small EMIs.

qa.q: What did Asif realise on adding up the EMIs?
qa.a: Asif was surprised at the total and saw that none of the purchases was a need; they came from a mood and from friends' new things.

qa.q: What rule did Asif set to avoid more debt for lifestyle spending?
qa.a: Any purchase waits a week, then the total cost is checked, and no new EMI is taken until two of the existing ones are cleared.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: Karthik may feel trusted for being told honestly, since Asif thanks Karthik for not laughing.

grounding: Easy credit and buy-now-pay-later feel harmless to Asif until small EMIs are tallied; Asif asks about need and delays purchases.

"Darshan, look, the new noise-cancelling headphones. Only fifteen hundred a month!"
"Jatin, that's the third 'only' this month."
"What do you mean?"
"The phone. The smartwatch. Now these. How many monthly payments are you on?"
Jatin opened his banking app and started counting. His smile faded. "Five. Wait, six. The sneakers."
"And how much do they add up to?"
He added it on his calculator. He went quiet. "Almost a third of my salary."
"Do you need these headphones?"
"My old ones work... Everyone at the office has these."
"So it's for looking like everyone at the office."
Jatin sighed. "Kind of."
"Put them in your cart and wait a week. If you still want them next Sunday, fine."
"A week?"
"A week. And write down every small EMI you have on one page."
Jatin closed the app. "Okay. Next Sunday."

qa.q: How many monthly payments was Jatin on?
What was Jatin feeling when he added up his payments?
qa.a: He felt shocked and uneasy, going quiet when he saw they came to almost a third of his salary.

qa.q: What did Darshan suggest Jatin try?
qa.a: Asking whether he needs the item, waiting a week before buying, and writing down every small EMI on one page.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Jatin's spending?
qa.a: Darshan seems concerned, noticing the "onlys" adding up and wanting Jatin to see the pattern before it steals his freedom.

grounding: Easy credit and status spending feel harmless; a friend helps the protagonist track small EMIs, question need, and wait a week before buying.

passage:
I'm Francis, and a year ago I was the guy with the latest everything. New phone on easy EMIs. Sneakers on buy-now-pay-later. A gaming chair I barely used. Each one felt small. "Only" nine hundred a month. "Only" twelve hundred.
Then one month my salary came and, after the auto-payments, I had almost nothing left for rent. I sat on the floor of my flat in Kochi and felt sick.
My friend Zubin came over and asked a simple question: "Which of these did you need?" I was honest. Maybe two.
Looking back, what helped was so boring. I wrote every EMI on one sheet and stuck it on my fridge. I made a rule for myself: anything non-essential waits a week in the cart. Most things I stopped wanting by day three.
It took eight months to clear the small EMIs. I still like nice things. But now I choose them.

qa.q: Where did Francis stick the sheet of EMIs?
What was Francis feeling on the floor of the flat?
qa.a: Francis felt sick and alarmed, realising the small payments left almost nothing for rent.

qa.q: What habits helped Francis get out of lifestyle debt?
qa.a: Writing every EMI on one sheet, asking whether each item was a need, and waiting a week before buying anything non-essential.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt asking the simple question?
qa.a: Zubin was probably worried but careful not to lecture, hoping one honest question would help Francis see the pattern.

grounding: Easy credit and status spending feel harmless until they add up; the protagonist tracks small EMIs, questions need and delays purchases.
